source: Fortunato et al. (2018) Science of science (PMC full text)
finding: The review says teams grow by an average of 17% per decade and cites refs 50 (Wuchty 2007) and 54 (Jones 2009). It gives no years, fields or base sizes for the 17%.
numbers: 17% per decade (as stated); refs 50 and 54. Same page: publications with extremely strong collaborators gain 17% more citations (ref 59, Petersen 2015).
quote: Teams are growing in size, increasing by an average of 17% per decade
limits: The same review uses 17% twice for two different things. The team-growth figure is a review summary, not a measured result in this text.
agent_relevance: Background only. Do not quote 17% as exact.

source: Wu, Wang, Evans (2019) Large teams develop and small teams disrupt (arXiv SI Fig S28)
finding: Wu's own supplement measures team growth. Mean team size for articles rose from 2 to 5.5 (1954-2014) and for patents from 1.7 to 2.7 (1976-2014). Small teams (3 or fewer) fell from 91% to 37% in papers and 94% to 74% in patents.
numbers: Papers: 2.75x over 6 decades is about 18% per decade compounded. Patents: 1.59x over 38 years is about 13% per decade. (Our arithmetic, not stated in the source.)
quote: The average team size of articles increased from 2 to 5.5 between 1954 and 2014
limits: Web of Science and patent data. Compounding is our calculation. Growth is not constant per decade.
agent_relevance: Supports a rate in the range 13-18% per decade. The 17% is plausible for papers.

source: Jones (2009) The burden of knowledge and the death of the Renaissance man (Rev Econ Stud)
finding: Ref 54 of the Fortunato 17% line. Patent team size rose from 1.73 (1975) to 2.33 (1999), a 35% rise over 24 years. The trend holds with controls for technology class and foreign vs domestic patents.
numbers: 35% over 24 years is about 13% per decade compounded (our arithmetic). Sample 2.1 million US patents 1975-1999. Drugs class mean team 2.91.
limits: Patents only, ends 1999. Does not give 17%. Jones cites Wuchty 2007 for papers.
agent_relevance: So 17% per decade is not reproduced by this source. It gives about 13%.

source: Wuchty, Jones, Uzzi (2007) The increasing dominance of teams (Science), abstract via Crossref and OpenAlex
finding: Abstract confirms 19.9 million papers over 5 decades and 2.1 million patents, and that teams dominate in nearly all fields. The abstract has no per-decade growth number. The body text (team size 1.9 to 3.5) was paywalled and not read.
numbers: 19.9 million papers, 2.1 million patents. Cited by about 2,830 (Crossref) to 4,371 (OpenAlex).
quote: Teams typically produce more frequently cited research than individuals do
limits: Only the abstract was read. The 1.9 to 3.5 figure remains recalled, not verified. If true (about 45 years) it gives about 14-15% per decade.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays partly open. Direction firm, exact 17% not pinned to Wuchty.

source: Hao, Xu, Li, Evans (2025) AI tools expand scientists' impact but contract science's focus (arXiv v4, Nature-accepted text)
finding: The v4 arXiv text (marked just accepted by Nature) does contain the multipliers: AI-adopting scientists publish 3.02 times more papers, get 4.84 times more citations, and lead projects 1.37 years earlier. Topics shrink 4.63%. This settles the earlier doubt about whether the multipliers are real.
numbers: 3.02x papers (t=47.18), 4.84x citations (t=30.32), 1.37 years earlier to project lead, 4.63% smaller median knowledge extent. 27,405,011 papers with +98.70% annual citations; 5,377,346 researchers; 2,282,029 career trajectories.
limits: Observational. Raw multipliers are not causal. Same group (Evans) as Wu 2019 and Lin 2023.
agent_relevance: Individual gain with collective narrowing. Matches G10: keep exploration wide when one tool or one chain dominates.

source: Hao et al. (2025) selection control (arXiv v4 text on matched cohorts)
finding: The authors test selection into AI use. They match 11,019 scientists who adopted AI in career year 3 to 1,926 non-adopters with similar first-3-year citations. By year 10 the adopters have 24.45% higher annual citations and 9.61% higher productivity. A second cohort (9,837 who adopted in year 5) shows the same pattern.
numbers: +24.45% citations and +9.61% productivity at career year 10, versus 4.84x citations (+384%) in the raw comparison. So most of the raw gap is not retained after matching.
limits: Matching on early trajectory only. Hidden traits (funding, lab, ambition) not controlled. Matched group is much smaller than the adopter group.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 mostly closed: the multipliers are real in the source, but the matched effect is far smaller (tens of percent, not multiples).

source: Hao et al. (2025) AI and team size (arXiv v4)
finding: AI-augmented papers have smaller teams: 1.33 fewer scientists (19.29%). Junior scientists fall from 2.89 to 1.99 (31.14%), established scientists from 4.01 to 3.58 (10.77%). Junior adopters reach established status with probability 45.00%, 13.64% above non-adopters.
numbers: t=20.47 for team size; t=19.02 juniors; t=20.82 established. Transition gain tested on 6 disciplines (significant on 4 of 6, p<0.2 stated).
limits: Association only. Fewer juniors may reflect tool substitution or topic choice.
agent_relevance: Direct link to team science: AI may shrink teams. For the agent, tools substitute for headcount, not for diversity.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Towards a science of scaling agent systems (arXiv v3, frontier models)
finding: The 0.45 ceiling is fitted on data that includes frontier models (GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro and the smaller GPT-5 nano, Sonnet 3.7, Gemini 2.0 Flash), not only 7B-32B open models. Rule: multi-agent is advised only when single-agent accuracy is below about 0.45. It picks the right architecture for 87% of held-out configs versus 54% for a capability-only model.
numbers: beta = -0.236 (p=0.004); threshold 0.040/0.236 = 0.170 standardized, about 0.45 raw. Held-out frontier check on BrowseComp-Plus: MAS-only MAE 0.061, overall MAE 0.077. R2 0.373 overall, 0.413 with the task-grounded capability metric.
limits: Threshold is derived from the same 260 configs it is tested on (cross-validated). Held-out evidence is one benchmark. Authors say preliminary, not full cross-domain generalization. Gap 4 is partly closed: frontier models are in the fit, but no sweep varies one frontier model across accuracy levels.
agent_relevance: Use 0.45 as a prior, not a law. Branch only when base accuracy on the task is low.

source: Kim et al. (2025) heterogeneity figure 4 (arXiv v3)
finding: Mixing model capability is family-dependent. Anthropic: a low-capability orchestrator with high-capability sub-agents scores 0.42 versus 0.32 for all-high (+31%). OpenAI and Gemini degrade under the same mix. In decentralised debate, mixed beats all-high for OpenAI (0.53 vs 0.50) and Anthropic (0.47 vs 0.37), ties Gemini (0.42 vs 0.43).
numbers: BrowseComp-Plus, three model families, centralised vs decentralised. Sub-agent capability mattered more than orchestrator capability in all families.
limits: One benchmark; no confidence intervals in the caption.
agent_relevance: Relevant to gap 10: mixing helps or hurts depending on family and architecture, so quality gap alone is not the whole story.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop overvaluing multi-agent debate (arXiv 2502.08788, Heter-MAD)
finding: Heter-MAD randomly picks, at each agent call, one of two candidate models (GPT-4o-mini or Llama3.1-70b). Heter-SoM beats the average of SoM on each model alone by 6.4%, Heter-EoT beats EoT-average by 8.2%, and all MAD methods beat CoT-average by up to 5.8%. Gains are smaller for ChatEval and AgentVerse.
numbers: Nine benchmarks (MMLU to MBPP). Two candidate models of similar strength, mixed with equal probability.
quote: Heter-MAD consistently improves the performance of all considered MAD frameworks
limits: The baseline is the average of two models, not the best single one. A fair test against the best single model was not the headline.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: Zhang compares against the average, Li compares against the best single model. This difference alone explains much of the apparent conflict.

source: Li et al. (2025) Rethinking Mixture-of-Agents: is mixing different LLMs beneficial (Self-MoA, arXiv 2502.00674)
finding: MoA performance rises with both proposer quality and diversity, but is more sensitive to quality. Linear fits over about 70 mixtures per dataset: MMLU quality 2.558 vs diversity 1.841 (R2 0.771); CRUX 4.548 vs 1.421 (R2 0.685); MATH 4.719 vs 2.839 (R2 0.760). Self-MoA (best model sampled many times) beats mixed-MoA by 6.6 points on AlpacaEval 2.0 and 3.8 on average.
numbers: Over 200 experiments. Diversity by Vendi score, quality by mean proposer accuracy. At fixed quality, more diversity helps.
quote: MoA is quite sensitive to variations in quality
limits: Coefficients are normalised linear fits, not causal. Mixing six models of unequal quality is the main test.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 answer: largely a quality-gap effect. Diversity helps at fixed quality, but adding weaker models costs more than diversity gains. In-model sampling gives diversity without the quality loss.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail? (arXiv v3, Oct 2025)
finding: v3 separates two interventions on ChatDev with the same model: better role specification alone gives +9.4% success, and adding a high-level task-objective verification step gives +15.6% (the maximum). So the +9.4% belongs to role spec, and the +15.6% to verification. Failure modes include 3.2 no or incomplete verification, 3.3 incorrect verification, 3.1 premature termination, 1.5 unaware of termination, 1.3 step repetition.
numbers: 1,642 annotated traces, 7 MAS, failure rates 41% to 86.7%. The text lists category shares both as 44.2/32.3/23.5 and 41.8/36.9/21.3, so shares differ across figures.
quote: adding a high-level task objective verification step to ChatDev yields a +15.6% improvement
limits: Category shares are inconsistent inside the paper. Traces are multi-agent only.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 partly: modes 1.3, 1.5, 3.1, 3.2, 3.3 do not need a second agent. They can occur in one agent's own chain, so a stop rule and an external verification step are likely fixes. No single-agent trace study exists.

source: Bertalanic and Fortuna (2026) Ringelmann scaling for LLM teams (arXiv 2606.02646)
finding: The ceiling check on frontier models is thin. Frontier tests are Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite (c = 0.95 GSM-Hard, 0.86 GPQA) and Gemini 3.1 Pro at N=1 only (97.0% MMLU-Hard, 80.6% GSM-Hard, 88.9% GPQA), where the framework predicts c near 1 so no team run was made. Cross-family replication is within the same paper (Llama, Ministral).
numbers: 44 model-task-condition cells, R2 > 0.99. Qwen2.5-32B c = 0.96/0.77/0.97 vs 7B 0.85/0.57/0.81. Qwen3-8B thinking c = 1.00 at 87.2% solo.
limits: Single group, preprint. No independent group found. Frontier claim is a prediction, not a measured team curve. Frontier multi-agent runs deliberately omitted.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open: no independent replication. Consistent in direction with Kim's 0.45 ceiling.

source: Lin, Frey, Wu (2023) Remote collaboration fuses fewer breakthrough ideas (arXiv 2206.01878 full text)
finding: Reconciliation of the two counts. 20,134,803 papers (1960-2020) and 4,060,564 patents (1976-2020). The raw split is P(D>0) 28% to 22% for papers and 67% to 55% for patents (0 km to over 600 km). With full controls (field, period, team size, career age, knowledge diversity, tie strength, author fixed effects) it is 20.4% to 19.5% for papers and 58.2% to 56.5% for patents, about 3-4% relative. The D percentile 89 to 84 (papers) and 76 to 67 (patents) is the alternative measure in Extended Data Fig 3.
numbers: Same scientist conceives research 63% to 51% when remote; conceptual tasks 48% vs 42%. New concepts 0.40% to 0.32% (papers), new tech codes 3.33% to 3.22% (patents). 89,575 contribution disclosures.
limits: Not a conflict, three metrics: raw share, controlled share, mean percentile. The controlled effect is small (under 1 percentage point for papers). Same group as Wu 2019; no outside replication found. Uses the D score, which inherits the Holst zero-reference concern.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 closed on the counts; replication outside Wu's group stays open. Effect is real but small once controlled.

source: Holst et al. (2024) Dataset artefacts and the declining disruptiveness of science (arXiv 2402.14583), check for Wu 2019
finding: Holst cites Wu 2019 only in the reference list and does not rerun team-size results. So gap 1 is unanswered by Holst. Their mechanism: entries with zero references get CD5 = 1; a dummy for zero references removes the regression residual spike and the decline is gone for papers.
numbers: 972,161 papers and 142,362 patents with CD5 = 1; 97% of the paper CD5=1 cases and 78% of the patent cases have zero references in the databases.
limits: Wu 2019 used Web of Science and a different window. Its SI names exclusions only for review articles, not for zero-reference entries. Its controls include author fixed effects, journal, subfield and topic. No zero-reference filter is stated in the SI text we read.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open. Nobody has rerun Wu on filtered data. Risk is real but unmeasured.

source: Wu, Wang, Evans (2019) robustness text (arXiv SI)
finding: Wu's negative team-size effect is tested with author fixed effects, topic controls (100,000 articles' titles and abstracts), excluding reviews, journal and subfield controls, and with reference-based measures (reference age falls and reference popularity rises with team size). Reference-based measures are only defined for papers that list references.
numbers: Fixed-effect coefficient -0.00018 vs random effects -0.00027 (about two thirds retained).
limits: This does not test zero-reference removal. It does show the pattern appears in more than one metric, which lowers (but does not remove) the Holst risk.
agent_relevance: Indirect support for K01 while gap 1 stays open.
